summary: Billie Jean King, turning 80 in November 2023, continues to push for investment and equity in women's sports, saying the field is at a "tipping point" as people see it as a great investment. The AP piece covers her recent activities, her ownership stakes, the 50th anniversary of equal prize money at the U.S. Open and the King-Riggs match, and a Q&A on women's hockey, investment and media coverage. She says women's sports get only about 5% of media coverage and that this must change.
one_line: At nearly 80, Billie Jean King says women's sports are at a tipping point for investment while citing only 5% media coverage as the key gap.
key_facts: Billie Jean King turns 80 in November 2023.

In the last three months King attended the Women's World Cup in Australia, kicked off the player draft for the new women's pro hockey league in Toronto, and is opening a London office for a tennis venture involving the Billie Jean King Cup.
King is part of ownership groups involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers, the NWSL's Angel City FC and the PWHL hockey league, which starts in January.

In summer 1973, at age 29, King established the WTA, won the Wimbledon triple crown (singles, doubles, mixed doubles), achieved equal pay at the U.S. Open and beat Bobby Riggs in the "Battle of the Sexes".
King and about 60 athletes were to celebrate the 50th anniversary of equal U.S. Open prize money and the King-Riggs match at her annual Women's Sports Foundation awards dinner in New York.
Barack and Michelle Obama attended the U.S. Open at Arthur Ashe Stadium in August to mark the pay equity milestone; Michelle Obama said it is about "how women are seen and valued in this world."
King launched the production company "Pressure is a Privilege" and is executive producer and host of the documentary "Groundbreakers," airing on PBS on Nov. 21.
Members of Congress are working to award King the Congressional Gold Medal.
The PWHL will have teams in Boston, New York, Minnesota, Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, and took five years to come together; Kendall Coyne asked King for help.
King says she asks CEOs whether they invest as much in women as in men, and it usually gets quiet, though she says it is better than it used to be.
King says male allies with money and power have made a big difference, and more women investors are coming in, particularly in soccer.
King says women's sports get only 5% of media coverage, which is where the money is, and that this has to change.
